Gemma: Get a cockapoo. Mine's called Biscuit. Actually, I just spoke to a fella from Warrington with a cockapoo called Biscuit as well, it was mad.
Joel: Warrington? I'm from Warrington! Great Sankey. Was he a Wolves fan?
Gemma: Yes! He had a magnet on the fridge.
Joel: Made up. There's a lot of us about. That'll have been him with the Wolves magnet, I spotted that in the photos.
Gemma: Small world. And I grew up in Derby, so I'm a Rams fan, loosely, more for the day out than the football.
Joel: That's the right way to do it, to be fair. I'm Liverpool for football, which gets me some stick in Manchester, so I'm not one to judge.
calls.C0432:
Craig: Hiya, can you hear me alright? I'm Craig, I'm in Warrington.
Jaspal: Hiya mate, yeah, loud and clear. Jaspal, Derby. I clocked the Wolves magnet on your fridge, so I'm guessing rugby league?
Craig: Rugby league, yeah, Warrington Wolves, born and bred. And I clocked your Derby shirt, so I'm guessing you suffer.
Jaspal: Suffer is the word, mate. I go with my cousin a few times a season and we moan about the board from the car park all the way down the A38. It's basically therapy. Do you follow the football as well?
Craig: Casually. Mainly so I've got something to say to clients, if I'm honest. I'm in sales, flooring, so half my day is "did you see the match?" with a facilities manager.
Jaspal: Ha, that's genius, that. I'm a teacher, Business and Economics, and I do the exact same with the lads at the back. You get them on the football and then you sneak inflation in.
Craig: Sneak inflation in, I like that. There was a dog's tail in your photo, wasn't there? Bottom corner.
Jaspal: That's Biscuit. My partner's dog, technically, but I do the walks. Reluctantly.
Craig: You're joking. Ours is called Biscuit. Cockapoo.
Jaspal: No way. Ours is a cocker spaniel, old lad now. Does yours eat socks?
Craig: Ate one last week! I was in the garden at ten at night with a torch.
Jaspal: Mate, same, we've had the vet bill and everything. It's like there's a national Biscuit conspiracy.
Craig: There must be, because that's three now. I had a call earlier with a physio, Gemma, from near Nottingham, and hers is a Biscuit as well.
Jaspal: Hang on, hang on. My partner's called Gemma. And she's a physio.
Craig: Stop it.
Jaspal: Swear down. Royal Derby, though, not Nottingham. Did she say anything about a handsome teacher?
Craig: Ha, she said she was married to a Dan, so I'd hope it's not her, mate.
Jaspal: I'd hope so too! Nine years and we're not married, so if she's gone and married a Dan behind my back I've got questions. Sorry, go on, what were you saying about work?
Craig: No, just the sales. Cheshire, Merseyside, Manchester, I'm on the M62 most of the week. Did three hundred miles this week. Five-a-side on a Wednesday's about the only fixed thing, and even that I sort of hobble round now with my ankle.
Jaspal: Wednesday five-a-side! Same night, me. I'm mostly there for the pint, to be fair. I say I'm a holding midfielder, which means I hold my position because I can't run.
Craig: Ha, that's me now. Since forty I've slowed right down. Cut back on the midweek beers and all. My dad had a heart scare a few months ago, and it sort of makes you think, you know.
Jaspal: Oh no, is he alright now?
Craig: He's doing better. On tablets, walking every day, my mum's got him on porridge, which he's not happy about.
Jaspal: Porridge, ha. My mum would sooner die than give my dad porridge. Everything's rice and bolani and ghee in our house. She sends me home with tubs every Sunday.
Craig: Bolani? What's that?
Jaspal: Afghan flatbread, stuffed, potato and leek usually. We're Afghan Sikh, came over when I was nine. Honestly, I make a decent karahi, but I can't touch my mum's bolani.
Craig: That sounds unbelievable. I'm a slow-cooker chilli man myself. Kerry does most of the teas, I do the Sunday roast, and the barbecue if there's any sun.
Jaspal: Barbecue the second it hits twelve degrees, I bet.
Craig: Fourteen. I'm not an animal.
Jaspal: Fair. Right, important question, what car are you getting next? Because I'm fancying one and I need talking out of it.
Craig: Oh, don't get me started, I'm choosing my next lease right now...
calls.C0433:
Gemma: Hiya! Can you hear me? I'm Gemma, I'm in Beeston, near Nottingham.
Kacper: Yeah. Kacper. Swindon.
Gemma: Swindon, lovely. Is that the one with the Magic Roundabout?
Kacper: Yeah, that one. It's fine once you know it.
Gemma: I'd be terrified. What do you do?
Kacper: Shift manager. Distribution centre, nights and weekends. About forty on my team.
Gemma: Nights! Oh God, how do you do it? I do a ten-hour clinic day and I'm knackered. I'm a physio, NHS outpatients, musculoskeletal, and I do private sports massage on Saturdays.
Kacper: You get used to it. Four on, four off. I'm on my days off now.
Gemma: Oh, so I'm keeping you from your bed, sorry! I could tell from your photo you're a gym person, with the shaker.
Kacper: Yeah, four times a week. PureGym, it's twenty-four hours, so I go whenever.
Gemma: See, I do reformer Pilates, twice a week in West Bridgford. The instructor's terrifying but amazing. Have you ever tried it?
Kacper: No. Seems expensive.
Gemma: Haha, it is, don't tell me mum. But honestly, for lifters it's brilliant, all your mobility and your core, it sort of stops you getting injured. I see so many gym lads in clinic with dodgy lower backs, do you know what I mean?
Kacper: My lower back's alright. Hips get tight sometimes, on squats.
Gemma: Hips, yeah, that's classic. Do you warm up properly or just go straight in?
Kacper: Erm. Bit of both.
Gemma: That's a no, then! You want some hip stretches before you squat, honestly, just five minutes. Sorry, I'll stop, I'm in work mode. Do you live on your own down there?
Kacper: With my sister and her husband. I rent their spare room. Saving for a deposit.
Gemma: Oh, that's nice. We've got a lodger, actually, so the other way round, he helps with the mortgage. He leaves the hob on. Please tell me you don't leave the hob on.
Kacper: No. I meal-prep, I'm pretty careful. Dan would kill me.
Gemma: Dan? My husband's called Dan!
Kacper: Right. It's a common name.
Gemma: Haha, fair enough. Everyone today's got something the same. Two people with dogs called Biscuit and everything. Are your family in Swindon as well, then?
Kacper: Yeah, my parents too. We came from Poland when I was ten. Gdańsk.
Gemma: Oh, I've heard Gdańsk is gorgeous. Is it worth a trip? I've been wanting somewhere a bit different. We did Santorini for our honeymoon, which was stunning, but I want somewhere less obvious next.
Kacper: It's nice. The old town. I go back once a year to see my grandparents. I want to do Dubai next, though.
Gemma: Ooh, Dubai. That's very fancy.
Kacper: A mate from work went. Looked good. Bit of a flashy one, yeah.
Gemma: I love a bit of flashy. Life's too short for budget airline queues. Did you ever do any sport besides the gym? Football or anything?
Kacper: Five-a-side for a bit. Stopped because of the rota. Mostly FIFA now, on PlayStation.
Gemma: Haha, that's basically five-a-side without the ankle injuries, isn't it. I had a fella earlier who does five-a-side on Wednesdays and...
calls.C0434:
Jaspal: Hiya! Can you hear me alright? Jaspal, Derby.
Gemma: Hiya! Yeah, I can hear you. I'm Gemma, I'm in Beeston, but I'm Derby born, so you're practically family.
Jaspal: Gemma! Right, I've got to tell you this. I had a call with Craig, Warrington lad, and he said he'd spoken to a physio called Gemma with a dog called Biscuit. And my partner is a physio called Gemma, and we've got a dog called Biscuit.
Gemma: Shut up. You're joking.
Jaspal: Swear down. So for about ten seconds I thought she'd joined the study and married a Dan behind my back.
Gemma: (laughs) Oh my God. I am married to a Dan! Is your Gemma at Nottingham?
Jaspal: No, Royal Derby. Cocker spaniel, old boy, eats socks. Yours?
Gemma: Cockapoo, chews phone chargers. So we're different Gemmas, you're safe. That's honestly mad though. Is she MSK?
Jaspal: Yeah, MSK. She'll probably know you, to be fair, it's a small world, physios.
Gemma: It really is. Tell her the Beeston Gemma says hi. And that the waiting list's from hell over here as well.
Jaspal: Oh, she says the same, word for word. Comes in after a long shift and just lies on the settee going "don't talk to me".
Gemma: That's me after a ten-hour clinic! I get home and lie on the floor with Biscuit. So what do you do? Let me guess, teacher, with all the textbooks?
Jaspal: Everyone gets that. Sixth form college, Business and Economics, on the edge of Derby. I run Young Enterprise as well, so the kids make stuff and try and sell it. Last year's lot did candles and they actually turned a profit, which I'll take full credit for, obviously.
Gemma: (laughs) Obviously. See, I'd love to know about business stuff. I want my own clinic eventually, private physio and Pilates, nice fit-out, proper Instagram, be my own boss, do you know what I mean?
Jaspal: Do it. Honestly. Half my job is telling seventeen-year-olds they can run a business, so I'd be a hypocrite if I said don't. What's stopping you?
Gemma: Erm, money, mainly. And I'm going for a Band 7 first. I'm doing private massage on Saturdays to build up clients, sort of thing.
Jaspal: That's sensible, that's the proper way. I've got a half-built idea for a tutoring company, and by half-built I mean it's a note on my phone.
Gemma: (laughs) That counts! Where in Derby did you grow up?
Jaspal: Littleover now, but we came over when I was nine, from Kabul via Delhi. Uncle had a shop on Normanton Road. Where were you?
Gemma: Allenton. Me mum and dad are still there. I went to sixth form in Derby, first in the family to go to uni, so me mum still tells everyone at the Co-op.
Jaspal: Ha, my mum's the same, she tells the whole gurdwara I'm basically running the college. I'm not, for the record. Do you still go to Pride Park?
Gemma: Now and again, with me dad. More for the day out, if I'm honest, the pie and that. He had a heart scare last year, so I like taking him when I can.
Jaspal: Yeah. That's nice, that. Is he doing alright?
Gemma: He's much better, thanks. He moans about the board the whole way home, so he must be.
Jaspal: That's how you know they're healthy, mate. Moaning about the board is the best medicine going.
calls.C0435:
Craig: Hiya, can you hear me? I'm Craig, I'm in Warrington.
Joel: Mate! I'm Joel, I'm from Warrington. Well, Manchester now, Levenshulme, but Great Sankey originally.
Craig: Great Sankey? That's where I live! I saw the Wolves shirt in your photo and I thought, he's one of ours.
Joel: Made up. And I saw the magnet on your fridge. Gemma said she'd had a fella from Warrington with a Wolves magnet and a cockapoo called Biscuit, so I knew it was you.
Craig: (laughs) The famous Biscuit. Turns out there's three of them in this study. Which bit of Great Sankey were you?
Joel: Near the leisure centre. My mum and dad are still there, I'm back most fortnights for Sunday dinner at my nan's.
Craig: You'll have driven past mine, then. Small world. Do you get to the Halliwell Jones much?
Joel: Handful of times a season, with my dad. Easter was grim, wasn't it.
Craig: Don't. Losing to Saints at Easter, I couldn't speak to anyone for two days. Kerry said I was mardy all weekend.
Joel: (laughs) My dad was the same. So what do you do?
Craig: Sales, commercial flooring. Carpet tiles, vinyl, offices, schools, care homes, all round Cheshire, Merseyside and Manchester. You?
Joel: Solicitor. Corporate, in town, mostly people selling businesses, share purchases, that sort of thing. My dad still asks when I'm getting a proper trade, he's a plumber.
Craig: (laughs) That's very Warrington, that. You'll have clients like mine, then, blokes who've run a firm thirty years.
Joel: Exactly that. Half of it's just them being nervous and wanting someone to talk to, you know. I had a completion go till midnight Tuesday, and I've still not recovered. Bacon barm the next morning was the only thing that got me through.
Craig: Sausage barm for me, on site. Regretted it every time. Do you play anything?
Joel: Five-a-side, Wednesday nights, cage pitch in Longsight. When deals allow, which is never. It got rained off last week anyway.
Craig: Wednesday! Me too. Well, I say play. Dodgy ankle, I'm more of a, you know, a presence.
Joel: (laughs) A presence. I'll use that. I do parkrun Saturdays as well, Platt Fields, when I'm not hungover.
Craig: Fair play. I've taken up golf, partly for clients, if I'm honest. Twenty-four handicap and happy there.
Joel: That's smart, to be fair. We've got partners at work who do the whole golf day thing and I just sort of nod along.
Craig: Get yourself a set, mate, best networking going. Do you think you'll stay in Manchester?
Joel: Probably. Looking to buy with my girlfriend in a couple of years, Stockport or Heaton Moor maybe. Not Warrington, don't tell my mum.
Craig: Your secret's safe. I'll tell her I've never met you.
calls.C0436:
Klára: Hi, can you hear me? I'm Klára, in London.
Kacper: Yeah. Kacper. Swindon.
Klára: Hi. Erm, is Kacper a Polish name?
Kacper: Yeah. I'm from Gdańsk. Came over when I was ten.
Klára: Oh, nice. I'm Czech, from Brno. So we are almost neighbours.
Kacper: Sort of. Do you speak any Polish?
Klára: A little. I understand some, but I can't really speak it. There's a Polish shop near me on Hoe Street, I go there for the bread. Proper rye bread. But last week they ran out of the good one.
Kacper: My mum makes her own. Sends tubs back with my sister. Pierogi, żurek.
Klára: Your mum makes żurek? Lucky. We have something similar. I make mostly soups, and svíčková for special days.
Kacper: Don't know that one.
Klára: It's beef with a cream sauce and dumplings. It takes all day. My husband loves it. What do you do in Swindon?
Kacper: Shift manager. Distribution centre, nights and weekends. Forty people.
Klára: Forty, that's a lot. Is it hard, managing people?
Kacper: It's alright. Mostly it's people calling in sick. Someone always calls in sick on a Saturday.
Klára: (laughs) I worked in a shop on Oxford Street, it was the same. Always Saturday. Now I'm at home with my son, he's three and a half.
Kacper: Right. Must be busy.
Klára: Yes. Today he woke me at half past five to tell me about a T. rex. So I'm a little tired.
Kacper: I'm knackered too. Finished nights yesterday.
Klára: So we are both tired. Do you speak Polish at home?
Kacper: With my mum, yeah. English everywhere else. I feel more Swindon, to be honest.
Klára: I understand. I speak Czech with my son, but he answers more and more in English. I worry he will lose it.
Kacper: My sister worries about that too. If she has kids. She says she'll only speak Polish to them.
Klára: It's hard to do. You need to be stubborn.
Kacper: Yeah. My mum was stubborn. That's probably why I still speak it.
Klára: Then she did a good job. Do you go back to Poland?
Kacper: Once a year. Fly from Bristol. See my grandparents.
Klára: I go from Stansted. Always the early flight, with a toddler. Terrible.
Kacper: Early flights are the worst. I'd rather drive.
Klára: To Gdańsk?
Kacper: No. Probably not. Bit far.
calls.C0437:
Jaspal: Hiya mate! Can you hear me? Jaspal, Derby.
Joel: Yeah, loud and clear. Joel, I'm in Manchester. Levenshulme.
Jaspal: Manchester, nice. I've been to the Etihad once for a cup game and we got battered, so I've got mixed feelings about the place.
Joel: (laughs) Don't worry, I'm Liverpool, so I've got mixed feelings about it as well. I get proper stick at work for it.
Jaspal: A Liverpool fan in Manchester? Brave man. What do you do?
Joel: Solicitor, corporate. Business sales mostly, share purchases. You're a teacher, I'm guessing? Gemma said there was a teacher in Derby with a dog called Biscuit.
Jaspal: Ha, the Biscuit thing's gone right round the study, hasn't it? Yeah, sixth form, Business and Economics. And the best bit is, my partner's a physio called Gemma as well. When Craig told me he'd met a physio called Gemma with a Biscuit, I genuinely had a moment.
Joel: Stop it. My girlfriend's a physio too! Hannah, MSK, NHS.
Jaspal: You're joking. Is everyone in this study going out with a physio?
Joel: Seems like it. She talks about the waiting list like it's a third person in the house.
Jaspal: Same! Gemma comes home and just goes "don't". That's the whole conversation. So corporate law, is that the all-nighters sort of thing?
Joel: Can be. Had a completion run till midnight Tuesday. Mostly it's fine, but when a deal's busy it's sixty hours a week, and you sort of just crack on. I try and keep Wednesday nights for five-a-side.
Jaspal: Wednesday five-a-side! That's me. Third person today that's said that, by the way. Craig does it, I do it, you do it.
Joel: (laughs) It's the national day for it. Are you any good?
Jaspal: Honestly? No. I'm there for the pint after. I tell people I'm a holding midfielder because I hold the one position and don't move. Do you play fantasy football?
Joel: Yeah, with uni mates. I'm losing, badly. Bottom three.
Jaspal: I run the one for staff at college, and I'll be honest, I'm second, and the bloke in first is the head of maths, so it's become a whole thing. He sends graphs.
Joel: Graphs? That's not on.
Jaspal: That's what I said! Spreadsheet warfare. Do you get out to anything in Manchester, comedy or that?
Joel: Frog and Bucket now and again. And gigs, Albert Hall, the Ritz. Hannah drags me to the big pop shows and I pretend I'm not enjoying it.
Jaspal: Ha, I love that. I go to the Glee Club in Nottingham, stand-up's my thing. Saw a lad there last time who did twenty minutes on Greggs and it was the best night of my life, nearly.
Joel: Greggs material always lands, to be fair. Where's home originally?
Jaspal: Kabul, if you go far enough back. Afghan Sikh, came over when I was nine. Derby ever since, though. You?
Joel: Warrington. Turns out Craig lives round the corner from my mum and dad, which was mad.
Jaspal: It's a village, this study. Right, what are you doing for holidays? Because I'm trying to talk Gemma into Benidorm with the lads and it's not going well.
Joel: (laughs) Benidorm's a hard sell. Mallorca with Hannah, most summers. Japan's on the list, if work ever calms down.
Jaspal: Japan, now that's a proper one. Sorry, go on, were you going to say something?
Joel: No, just, if it ever happens. Everyone I know says it'll calm down next year, and it never does, you know.
calls.C0438:
Gemma: Hiya! Can you hear me? I'm Gemma, Beeston, near Nottingham.
Klára: Hi, yes. I'm Klára, in Walthamstow. In London.
Gemma: Oh, I loved your photo, the little dinosaur on the sofa. How old is he?
Klára: Three and a half. Matěj. Dinosaurs are everything now. I know more about the T. rex than I ever wanted.
Gemma: (laughs) Honestly, that's adorable. And you saw my dog bed, I bet. Biscuit, the cockapoo.
Klára: Yes, I heard about Biscuit. Craig told me. He has a Biscuit too.
Gemma: Everyone has a Biscuit! I think there's three now. So are you at home with him full-time?

Gemma: Oh, you'd be brilliant on reception. I can just tell, you've got a calm face. Our receptionists at work are the ones who actually run the place, do you know what I mean? The patients shout at them, not at us.
Klára: (laughs) I'm used to shouting. On Oxford Street, people shouted about receipts.
Gemma: Then a physio reception would be a holiday for you. What I'd say, sorry, I'm going into advice mode, but get something on your CV, like a little admin course, because they do look at that.
Klára: Craig said this also. There's an online course I looked at. I just need to, erm, actually press the button.
Gemma: Press the button! I'll be checking. Is it hard, being at home all day? I always wonder.

Klára: No, it's okay. There's no right time. We waited a long time too, and people asked.

Gemma: Ah, thank you! That's the one corner I tidied for the camera, to be fair. I'm going to London to see Wicked soon, actually, my annual West End weekend.
Klára: Then you can come to Walthamstow and see the wallpapers.
Gemma: I might! Where are you from originally, Klára?
Klára: Brno, in Czech Republic. I came for one year, in 2014, and then I met my husband.
Gemma: That's so romantic. One year turned into forever.
Klára: Yes, sort of. And now the forever has a dinosaur.
calls.C0439:
Craig: Hiya, can you hear me alright? I'm Craig, Warrington.
Kacper: Yeah. Kacper. Swindon.
Craig: Kacper, nice one. I've heard a bit about you, actually. Gemma said you're the night shift man.
Kacper: Yeah. Shift manager, distribution centre. Nights and weekends.
Craig: Fair play. How many on your team?
Kacper: About forty.
Craig: Forty, that's a lot of people to keep happy at three in the morning. What's the trick?
Kacper: Erm. Don't really keep them happy. Just get the shift out on time. If the numbers are good, the site manager's happy, so.
Craig: (laughs) Honest answer, that. I'm in sales, flooring, so my whole job is keeping people happy. Facilities managers mostly. I let them moan, they sign the order.
Kacper: Makes sense. Do you get a car with it?

Kacper: What are you looking at?

Kacper: Yeah. I've got a BMW 1 Series, leased. If you're doing high mileage, check the excess mileage charges. Some of the company leases are fine, but if it's personal contribution, the BIK on the bigger engines kills you. Electric's better for tax. I looked at all of it before I got mine.
Craig: See, that's useful, that. The tax on the diesels is a killer, you're right. I did three hundred miles this week alone.
Kacper: Electric probably works out then. If you can charge at home.
Craig: I've got a drive, so I could. Kerry'll be made up if it saves money. Do you keep yours clean? You look like a man who keeps his car clean.
Kacper: Valeted every couple of weeks.
Craig: Mine's got a sausage barm wrapper in the footwell and a hi-vis vest on the back seat, if I'm honest. Are you after the next step up at work, then?
Kacper: Operations manager. Within three years. On days. I'm looking at other places too, Amazon, Iceland. Whoever pays more.
Craig: No loyalty, I like it. I've actually had a rival sniffing about, hinting at a better package. I'm sort of using it to get regional manager where I am, you know.
Kacper: That's what I'd do. Get the offer in writing first, though.
Craig: In writing, yeah, good shout. You're good at this. Do you still play football at all? Everyone today's a Wednesday five-a-side man.
Kacper: Used to. Stopped because of the rota. Gym now, four times a week.
Craig: I clocked the shaker. I've got a dodgy ankle, so I just sort of stand in the middle now.
Kacper: You should do some balance work for that.
Craig: That's what Gemma said! Standing on one leg brushing my teeth.
Kacper: Yeah. She told me about my hips. She doesn't stop.
Craig: (laughs) She's a free physio, to be fair, I'm not complaining.

C0432.line_text: Oh no, is he alright now?
C0432.what: Jaspal's smile drops and his eyes move off the screen to the small framed photo of an older couple on the bookshelf behind him. He holds that look for about two seconds before turning back to the camera, and his voice is quieter than before as he asks the question.
